subtitle: Leaders play a real part in employee resource groups. Learn to support employees’ connection and contribution through a clear purpose, practical arrangements and follow-through people can trust.
scope: For DHS leaders engaging with employee resource groups. Minnesota enterprise ERGs have their own current MMB guidelines, FAQs and bylaws; use those and responsible agency guidance for actual participation, leadership roles, time and approval. This course does not form a group, grant authority, negotiate employment terms or create a complaint process. All cases are practice and avoid community-specific teaching.
introTranscript: Employee resource groups can offer connection, learning and a place to contribute ideas about the workplace. Leaders can support that value without taking over the group, assigning its members responsibility for every inclusion issue or treating attendance as proof of commitment. This course examines purpose, participation arrangements, leader relationships, useful input, learning connections and responsible review. It distinguishes a group’s contribution from management, HR and formal processes. Staff remain responsible for their work, and the Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant provides program leadership, guidance and feedback. Actual group arrangements follow their current rules rather than the practice planning choices used here.

lessons.title: Understand the group’s purpose without making it represent everyone
lessons.summary: Clarify what an employee resource group can contribute and which responsibilities remain elsewhere.
lessons.objective: Explain a resource group’s contribution through a specific workplace purpose.
objectives: Explain a resource group’s contribution through a specific workplace purpose.
Distinguish a group perspective from a claim about every employee in a community.
Identify a concern that belongs in a responsible formal process rather than the group.
takeaways: A group can connect people and ideas.
Formal workplace responsibilities remain in their proper routes.
lessons.statement: An employee resource group offers contribution; it does not become the owner of every inclusion issue.

image.caption: A clear purpose helps leaders support contribution without assigning an extra burden.

intro.heading: Begin with the actual group and its purpose
intro.body:
A leader may hear “employee resource group” and imagine a social club, a policy committee or the representative voice of an entire community. Those assumptions can lead to either dismissing the group or giving it responsibilities it does not have. Begin with the actual group’s current purpose, rules and appropriate contact. Minnesota enterprise ERGs have public MMB guidance; local arrangements should not be assumed to match every enterprise rule.

Connection and learning can have professional value. Colleagues may exchange work experience, discover useful development resources and contribute ideas about a workplace arrangement. The value should be described through a real purpose rather than a guarantee that a group will eliminate every disparity or prevent all departures. A respectful leader asks what the group is trying to accomplish and how support would help.

Members do not represent every employee who shares an identity or background. A group may contain disagreement and several experiences. Someone may choose not to join and still value an inclusive workplace. Do not use membership or attendance to infer identity, commitment, potential or an individual intercultural orientation. Neither should members be assigned compulsory cultural education for the whole team.

Keep responsibilities clear. Management owns decisions within its authority. HR and designated offices handle formal employment and concern processes. The enterprise guidelines set boundaries on bargaining and grievances; the learning activities here do not create another route around those processes. If a formal issue arises, explain the responsible route rather than asking the group to investigate it.

Use an appropriate introduction: describe the group’s purpose, current contact and way to learn more, with actual participation requirements explained through the responsible process. Avoid promising unrestricted work time or assuming membership. Supporting a group begins with understanding it, not with declaring what its members should do for management.

lessons.keyStatement: A group’s input is a contribution to examine, not a universal account or a transfer of management responsibility.

flashcards.back: An employee collective with a defined purpose and current governing arrangements; enterprise groups use MMB guidance.
An expectation that one person or group must explain or speak for everyone with a shared identity.
Leadership assistance offered within the group’s rules and the leader’s actual authority.
The responsible process for an employment, accommodation, complaint or other official matter.
Optional development that remains distinct from required training and formal employment expectations.

items.title: The group is only a social activity
items.body: Connection can support useful work relationships and learning. Ask about the actual purpose before dismissing it. Do not claim a guaranteed retention or performance effect; describe the contribution and examine its usefulness. The group’s current guidance determines its arrangement, not a supervisor’s informal impression.

items.title: The group speaks for everyone
items.body: Members may share a focus while holding different experiences and views. Summarize input with its scope and preserve meaningful disagreement. Do not assume that a nonmember rejects inclusion or that one group response establishes every employee’s needs. Wider decisions may require other relevant perspectives.

items.title: The group will solve every workplace concern
items.body: A group can raise an idea or point to a barrier without owning the formal response. Leaders and designated offices retain their responsibilities. Explain the appropriate route for actual concerns, and do not ask members to investigate colleagues or negotiate matters outside the group’s purpose.

tabs.label: Group
tabs.body: The group offers contribution within its current purpose and rules. Members can share useful experience without representing every nonmember or becoming compulsory educators. Explain the scope of an invitation so the group’s input can matter without being presented as a universal endorsement. Meaningful participation respects both the contribution and what it cannot establish.

tabs.label: Leader
tabs.body: The leader supports appropriate activity and remains responsible for decisions within their role. Asking an ERG to certify that every employee’s needs are met transfers credibility without supplying complete evidence. Consider the group’s input alongside other relevant information, respond to it and explain the actual decision. Support should not depend on members praising a predetermined conclusion.

tabs.label: Responsible office
tabs.body: The responsible office handles formal employment, bargaining, grievance, accommodation and other specialized matters through their own processes. A resource group does not become an informal tribunal or a place to collect private case records. Clarifying this boundary preserves access to formal routes while allowing the group to identify a non-identifying workplace issue suitable for discussion.

check.question: A director asks one resource group to certify that a change meets every employee’s needs. What should change?
check.correct: Treat the group’s input as scoped contribution, examine other relevant evidence and retain the director’s responsibility for the decision.
wrong: Assume group members can speak for every nonmember.
Make group attendance mandatory before employees may comment.
Give the group responsibility for investigating all related workplace concerns.
check.feedbackCorrect: This values the contribution without exaggerating representation or transferring formal responsibilities.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Members cannot represent every nonmember’s experience. Compulsory attendance turns contribution into a gate for being heard. Assigning every workplace investigation to a group substitutes an improvised process for formal responsibility. Treat the input as scoped evidence, seek other relevant perspectives and retain the director’s actual decision duty.

sorting.heading: Identify the role of the group

items.text: Share ideas about making a development invitation clearer.
Certify the views of every employee with a shared background.
Handle a formal workplace allegation through the designated process.
Offer a learning conversation within the group’s purpose.
Provide all cultural education because members share an identity.
Determine an appointment through applicable HR procedures.

lessons.next: Next, make participation arrangements practical and accurate.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Director Sonia receives a resource group’s suggestions about project invitations. She says the group has now certified that every employee feels included and asks it to investigate a colleague’s complaint. The group offered a process idea, not those responsibilities.
options: Keep the statement because it sounds supportive.
Describe the suggestions accurately, examine relevant evidence and route the formal concern to its responsible process.
responses: Supportive language can still overstate representation and transfer duties improperly.
This values the actual input while preserving evidence and formal responsibilities.
Contribution can remain useful when its purpose and boundaries are clear.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice group introduction with purpose, scoped contribution, current contact route and responsibilities that remain elsewhere.

move.control: You can understand the group, describe its contribution and respond within actual authority.
move.failure: A group is either dismissed or made responsible for everyone’s inclusion and formal concerns.
move.next: Before the next request to a resource group, clarify the purpose and what responsibility remains with the requester.

lessons.title: Support participation through clear arrangements
lessons.summary: Explain applicable rules and practical workload considerations without inventing unlimited approval or pay promises.
lessons.objective: Identify the responsible source for actual participation and leadership requirements.
objectives: Identify the responsible source for actual participation and leadership requirements.
Discuss a practical workload arrangement without an identity-based assumption.
Write a response that explains the decision and appropriate guidance route.
takeaways: Use the current group and agency requirements.
Avoid unsupported promises or private assumptions.
lessons.statement: Support should be practical and consistent with the rules that actually apply.

image.caption: A clear discussion connects the activity, time and actual participation requirements.

intro.heading: Make the arrangement understandable
intro.body:
A supervisor may support a group in principle while leaving employees uncertain about attendance, leadership roles or time. Another supervisor may promise that every activity is automatically paid and approved. Both approaches create avoidable confusion. Use the current group rules, MMB enterprise guidance where applicable and responsible agency advice for the actual arrangement. The course’s practice examples do not create a blanket approval or compensation rule.

Ask what activity the employee wants to attend or support. Clarify the purpose, timing, commitment and relevant requirements. Group leadership can involve a different responsibility from attending one learning event. Explain the applicable route rather than assuming that all participation arrangements are identical. If uncertain, obtain current HR or program guidance before making a promise.

Discuss work coverage and deadlines through a consistent, relevant approach. A service function may need a workable coverage plan; an employee may need to coordinate an approved learning activity. Do not assume that someone’s identity means the event is either essential for them or unnecessary. Ask about the actual activity and responsibilities, and let the employee explain their interest without requiring a personal cultural story.

Make the response understandable. If an arrangement needs adjustment, explain the work reason and appropriate next option rather than using a vague lack-of-fit judgment. Do not invent an unrestricted right, a general prohibition or a new waiting period based on this course. Questions about time, pay, leadership approval or disputes belong with the responsible current guidance.

Check the practical result. Does the employee know the route, what information is needed and how the proposed arrangement fits the work? A public statement of support is not enough if people cannot use it. A clear, accurate discussion can support participation without bypassing responsibilities or making optional involvement a hidden performance requirement.

inThisLesson: Explain the response and guidance route.
lessons.keyStatement: Accurate support explains the applicable arrangement instead of promising or prohibiting everything at once.

items.title: An employee wants a group leadership role
items.body: Check the current role requirements and applicable supervisor or program process. Explain the commitment and discuss work arrangements honestly. Do not treat leadership as identical to occasional attendance or make a promise before the responsible requirements are understood.

items.title: An event overlaps a service responsibility
items.body: Examine actual coverage, deadlines and approved options using the current guidance. Avoid automatic identity-based assumptions or a vague refusal. A practical work question can be resolved more credibly when the reason, options and appropriate guidance route are explained.

items.title: An event extends beyond ordinary hours
items.body: Time and compensation questions can depend on actual circumstances and applicable agreements. Do not improvise a universal rule from a learning scenario. Use the current enterprise guidance and responsible HR advice, and avoid asking an employee to accept an unauthorized promise.

tabs.label: Activity
tabs.body: An activity description identifies what the employee wants to do and the relevant group purpose. Participation in an event may differ from holding a leadership role under current guidance. Check the actual arrangement rather than relying on memory of another activity. This gives the supervisor a real question to resolve instead of creating a blanket permission or prohibition.

tabs.label: Work
tabs.body: The work discussion addresses responsibilities, coverage and authorized time arrangements. A useful response connects those practical matters to current rules rather than to private identity assumptions. Ask what is needed to make participation workable, without requiring someone to prove group identity. Support can be clear and consistent while recognizing that different roles or activities may have different conditions.

tabs.label: Response
tabs.body: The response explains the approved arrangement or the responsible guidance still needed. An unrestricted promise may exceed authority, while a total prohibition avoids examining a legitimate request. State what is known and how the remaining question will be answered. Do not invent compensation, membership or paid-time rules to make the response sound settled.

check.question: A supervisor is unsure whether a proposed event and leadership role have different approval requirements. What should happen?
check.correct: Check current applicable guidance and responsible agency advice, then explain the actual requirements and workable arrangements.
wrong: Promise unrestricted paid participation for every possible activity.
Prohibit all involvement because the distinction is unclear.
Ask the employee to prove their identity before considering the request.
check.feedbackCorrect: This gives accurate support without inventing a rule or treating private identity as the decision criterion.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Unrestricted paid participation is a rule the supervisor may not have authority to create. Prohibiting all involvement avoids resolving the actual question. An identity test adds private criteria unrelated to practical requirements. Check current guidance and responsible agency advice, then explain the specific event or role arrangement accurately.

items.text: Confirm current leadership-role requirements through the appropriate guidance.
Every group event always has unlimited paid approval.
The employee must want the event because of their presumed identity.
Discuss service coverage and explain an appropriate next option.
No new employee may ever participate, based only on this course.
A nonmember must not care about inclusion.

lessons.next: Next, support the group without taking control of its voice.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Employee Emilio asks supervisor Paige about attending a learning event and later taking a group role. Paige does not know the current requirements and is tempted to approve both with an unlimited time promise. A service deadline also needs coverage.
options: Check current participation and role guidance, discuss the actual commitment and coverage, and explain the appropriate arrangement without a blanket promise.
Reject both requests because they require a conversation.
Ask Emilio to disclose personal background before reviewing the activity.
responses: This addresses the real questions and supports a usable arrangement within responsible authority.
An automatic refusal avoids the work question rather than explaining it.
Private background is not a substitute for the actual activity and requirements.

lessons.transfer: Draft a practice response to a participation request with activity, current-guidance question, work arrangement, explanation and next contact route.

move.control: You can obtain current guidance and discuss relevant work arrangements consistently.
move.failure: Employees receive symbolic support but unclear or unsupported participation terms.
move.next: Check the current guidance before the next participation or group-role discussion.

lessons.title: Offer leadership support without taking over
lessons.summary: Agree on a useful leader role while respecting group agency, honest limits and decision accountability.
lessons.objective: Describe one form of leader support connected to the group’s stated need.
objectives: Describe one form of leader support connected to the group’s stated need.
Identify sponsorship that controls the group’s message or agenda.
Write a support agreement with responsibility and limits.
takeaways: Leadership influence does not own the group.
lessons.statement: Support gives people usable help; control requires them to say what the leader wants to hear.

image.caption: A support role should have a clear purpose and limits.

intro.heading: Ask before offering a solution
intro.body:
A leader can provide access, help resolve practical barriers or connect a group’s idea to a responsible decision-maker. The same influence can silence the group when the leader insists on approving every message, selecting every topic or treating disagreement as ingratitude. Begin with the group’s stated purpose and need, and use its current rules to understand the appropriate leader role.

Ask what support would be useful. A group may need a clear contact for a process question, suitable meeting arrangements or a response to a workplace suggestion. Do not assume that a high-profile speech is the most valuable contribution. A modest, reliable action can be more useful than visibility that brings no practical change.

Explain what the leader can and cannot do. An executive sponsor or other supporter may have influence but not authority over every issue. Do not guarantee policy approval, employment outcomes or resources outside the role. If a request needs another authority, name the responsible route and what the leader will do to help the request reach it.

Preserve space for disagreement and member-led contribution within actual rules. A leader should not require the group to endorse a predetermined management conclusion as the price of support. Nor should the group be expected to absorb a leader’s decision responsibility. The leader can listen and respond while remaining accountable for decisions they make.

Set a practical agreement. Name the support, owner, appropriate contact, boundary and check of the result. Follow actual group governance and agency requirements rather than inventing a universal sponsor charter. Ask whether the arrangement helped and revise it if it created extra burden or reduced the group’s ability to contribute honestly.

lessons.keyStatement: A leader can support and respond without owning every agenda or borrowing the group’s credibility.

items.title: The leader offers only a speech
items.body: A speech can be welcome, but ask whether it addresses the actual need. If the group needs a response route or usable arrangements, follow through on that request within authority. Do not mistake public visibility for practical support or claim that the event itself resolves a workplace barrier.

items.title: The leader requires a favorable message
items.body: Making support conditional on endorsement undermines honest contribution. Explain actual communication and governance requirements without using them as a pretext for suppressing disagreement. A group can offer a scoped perspective while the leader retains responsibility for deciding and responding.

items.title: The request exceeds the leader’s authority
items.body: State the limit honestly and identify the appropriate route. Offer only the action you can carry out, such as obtaining a response from a responsible role. Do not promise an outcome or assign the unresolved work back to members without explaining who owns the decision.

tabs.label: Need
tabs.body: A need describes the barrier or opportunity the group identifies. The leader’s preferred photo opportunity may not address it. Ask what support would make the planned contribution usable and why. A specific need, such as access to a suitable meeting space through approved arrangements, provides a better basis than assuming visibility itself is the group’s desired result.

tabs.label: Role
tabs.body: A role states what the leader can actually do and which group arrangements apply. Offering help does not confer control over every member’s view or transfer management responsibility to the group. Keep formal decisions with authorized roles. Resources conditioned on endorsing a management conclusion undermine honest contribution rather than demonstrating a collaborative relationship.

tabs.label: Check
tabs.body: A check examines whether support proved useful. Invite candid feedback about the practical arrangement without making praise a condition of fair treatment. A delivered resource may still fail to support the activity. The leader can revise their own support while respecting the group’s purpose, boundaries and independent contribution within its actual rules.

check.question: A sponsor offers resources only if the group endorses a predetermined management conclusion. What is the concern?
check.correct: Support is being used to control the group’s contribution rather than enable honest input within its actual purpose and rules.
wrong: Every sponsor automatically owns every member’s opinion.
An endorsement proves the decision is evidence-based.
The group should become responsible for the leader’s decision.
check.feedbackCorrect: The problem is the conditional control and transfer of credibility, not the existence of a leader relationship itself.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A sponsor does not own every member’s opinion. An endorsement obtained as a condition of support does not establish evidence or independent agreement. Making the group responsible for the leader’s decision shifts authority without justification. Support honest input within the group’s purpose and actual rules, preserving management accountability.

items.text: Help the group reach the responsible process owner for a scoped question.
Require members to endorse the conclusion before support is offered.
Explain that the requested employment decision needs its formal route.
Confirm suitable meeting arrangements through approved channels.
Claim the group supports every decision because a sponsor attended once.
Promise only the contact and follow-through within the leader’s role.

lessons.next: Next, connect group ideas to a real decision opportunity.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Sponsor Kieran is asked to help a group obtain a response to a development-access suggestion. He instead schedules a speech and asks the group to praise the current system. The suggestion needs an answer from its process owner.
scenario.prompt: What would make the support useful?
options: Insist that praise is the price of sponsorship.
Ask about the needed response, connect the request to the responsible owner and explain Kieran’s actual follow-through role.
Transfer the owner’s decision responsibility to the group.
responses: This turns support into control and does not address the request.
This aligns support with the need and keeps responsibility and authority clear.
Members can contribute without becoming responsible for a management decision.

lessons.transfer: Draft a practice support agreement with need, leader action, authority limit, responsible contact and usefulness check.

move.control: You can provide practical assistance and honest routes without taking over the group’s voice.
move.failure: Sponsorship produces favorable publicity while the group’s actual request remains unanswered.
move.next: Ask the next group you support what practical action would help before proposing your own event or message.

lessons.title: Invite input while a decision can still change
lessons.summary: Create a scoped opportunity for contribution and explain what happened to the ideas received.
lessons.objective: State a decision question and the influence available to group input.
objectives: State a decision question and the influence available to group input.
Identify a consultation request made after the decision is settled.
Write a response that distinguishes an accepted change, a limitation and a next investigation.
takeaways: Invite it before the choice is settled.
lessons.statement: A request for ideas should offer a real decision opportunity rather than a request for endorsement.

image.caption: A meaningful invitation identifies the decision, available influence and response owner.

intro.heading: Connect contribution to the decision
intro.body:
A resource group may be invited to comment on a workplace change after the design is complete. The leader describes this as engagement, but members can only endorse or object to a settled choice. A meaningful request explains the decision question, what remains open, what is constrained and when input can influence the work. It also names who decides and who will return the response.

Choose a question that fits the group’s purpose and available experience. For example, a group could examine whether a development invitation is understandable and whether its interest route is usable. It should not be asked to certify legal compliance, represent every employee or substitute for the responsible agency equity analysis. Broader decisions may need additional evidence and other relevant perspectives.

Provide understandable material and appropriate time through current arrangements. Explain the proposed change in familiar terms and identify the specific choices. A large technical packet without an open question can create work without a usable chance to contribute. Do not require identity disclosure or personal harm accounts when a process review can answer the question.

Examine suggestions and preserve disagreement. A majority preference may be useful but does not erase a consequential minority concern. State the scope of input and evidence limits. Route formal matters through their responsible processes rather than treating them as suggestions the decision-maker can simply accept or reject.

Return an honest response. Explain which idea changed the work, which could not be adopted and why, and what needs further examination. The explanation should be understandable without exposing private information. If the decision was already fixed, say so rather than calling agreement a result designed together. Credible follow-through helps staff see how contribution connects to practical action.

Where a supporting leader is a manager or supervisor, MMB Policy 1436 requires immediate reporting of protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents to human resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. Follow current agency procedures and appropriate information handling. A support relationship or group discussion cannot postpone the duty, replace the formal route or promise absolute confidentiality.

inThisLesson: Explain the response and next step.
lessons.keyStatement: Input is meaningful when its possible influence and actual response are visible.

items.title: The decision is already settled
items.body: Be honest about whether the activity is information-sharing or a genuine request to influence a choice. Do not ask for endorsement while claiming shared design. If a future decision remains open, state that opportunity clearly and explain the existing constraint without inventing authority.

items.title: The group is asked for a compliance certificate
items.body: Members can contribute experiences and process observations, but their participation does not replace legal, HR or required equity-analysis responsibilities. Identify the actual question and responsible review route. Do not use a group’s credibility to certify a conclusion outside its role.

items.title: The response omits a minority concern
items.body: A less common view may identify an important access barrier. Preserve its meaning and explain the action, limitation or further inquiry. Do not present majority preference as proof that every issue is resolved, and handle any personal information through approved processes.

tabs.label: Invitation
tabs.body: An invitation describes the question, choices still open, constraints and decision owner. Input gathered after a decision is final cannot honestly be called shared design of that decision. Explain whether the activity is information, future input or a real current opportunity to influence. Accurate scope makes participation more useful than a generous label unsupported by the process.

tabs.label: Examination
tabs.body: Examination connects suggestions to the actual work and preserves differing reasons. Advice can improve a design without authorizing the group to decide a formal case. If a manager becomes aware of protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents, Policy 1436 requires immediate reporting to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. Group discussion cannot substitute for or postpone that duty.

tabs.label: Response
tabs.body: A response explains what changed, what did not and why, with an owner for follow-through. Attending a meeting does not prove members agreed or that all employees were represented. Keep private accounts out of the broad summary. A reasoned response can respect an unadopted suggestion without claiming that every recommendation was incorporated.

check.question: A leader asks for feedback after a policy decision is complete but calls the result shared design. What should be corrected?
check.correct: Explain the actual limits of the activity and distinguish information or future input from influence over the already completed decision.
wrong: Keep the label because any meeting counts as shared design.
Ask the group to endorse the choice to remove disagreement.
Treat the group’s attendance as a compliance certificate.
check.feedbackCorrect: This makes the participation promise accurate and leaves room for a genuine future decision opportunity.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A meeting after completion cannot establish shared design of the completed decision. Requiring endorsement removes rather than examines disagreement. Attendance does not supply a compliance certificate. Correct the participation promise, explain current limits and identify any genuine future decision that remains open to meaningful input.

items.text: The invitation identifies a choice that remains open and who decides.
Members are asked to agree to a settled design while it is called shared design.
The owner explains what changed and why another suggestion needs examination.
Materials show the open question and usable ways to respond.
The group is told to praise the conclusion before receiving the material.
A minority concern is preserved with a stated follow-through action.

lessons.next: Next, connect group learning to everyday work without making membership an access gate.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Process owner Laila asks a group to review a new project invitation. The interest route can still change, but the job requirements cannot be changed in this discussion. One member identifies a confusing instruction that others did not notice.
options: State the open choice and constraints, examine the instruction concern and explain the resulting change or further inquiry.
Discard the concern because most members did not mention it.
Claim the group approved every employment requirement.
responses: This offers real influence and returns a scoped, evidence-based response.
A less common concern may still identify a real barrier.
The group’s process observation is not a universal approval or formal certification.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice input invitation with decision, open choice, constraints, owner and response route. Draft a response to one accepted suggestion and one unresolved question.

move.control: You can offer a genuine opportunity within authority and explain what happens to input.
move.failure: The group supplies time and credibility but receives no honest account of its influence.
move.next: Before requesting group input, confirm that the choice is open and name the response owner.

lessons.title: Connect learning and relationships to work
lessons.summary: Help employees use relevant learning while preserving open access, optional participation and formal training distinctions.
lessons.objective: Connect one learning activity to a practical work capability.
objectives: Connect one learning activity to a practical work capability.
Distinguish optional learning from required training credit or employment expectations.
Identify an access route that unnecessarily depends on group membership.
takeaways: Learning should have a usable work connection.
Relevant resources should not depend on presumed identity.
lessons.statement: A group can help people discover learning without becoming the only door to useful resources.

image.caption: A practical learning activity connects an idea with an action people can try.

intro.heading: Make the connection useful without making it compulsory
intro.body:
A resource group can introduce a useful idea, contact or learning activity. The leader’s role is to help employees understand how it relates to their work and where appropriate support is available. That connection should not make group membership a condition of using the wider program or turn optional participation into a measure of commitment. People can learn and contribute through several routes.

Name the capability the activity supports. A discussion about project invitations might help someone write clearer criteria or check who can discover an opportunity. A conversation about communication could lead to a practice of separating observed words from an assumed motive. The value is more visible when the employee can try a concrete action and reflect on its effect.

Keep the actual course, guided practice and group discussion distinct. A group event may introduce a resource but does not automatically replace a complete course or agency-required training. Program participation does not count toward DHS-required training credit unless expressly approved by the responsible leadership. Explain current credit and attendance requirements through their actual sources rather than making a promise based on the event’s title.

Preserve open learning access. Staff anywhere in DHS can use appropriate One DSD resources as they see fit. Do not require group membership, a cultural disclosure or an inferred developmental stage before a person may read a relevant resource. Actual protected workspaces and formal employment duties may have their own legitimate requirements; optional learning does not create a new gate.

Offer follow-through that builds independent capability. A colleague can apply an idea, examine a result and request consultant guidance or another responsible contact when useful. The consultant leads the program and supports staff with knowledge and feedback; staff perform their own work. A group connection should strengthen that ecosystem without making members responsible for carrying every learning or equity task for everyone else.

lessons.keyStatement: A learning connection offers a usable next step without making membership or optional participation an employment test.

items.title: An event title sounds like required training
items.body: A familiar topic does not determine training-credit status. Check the actual agency requirement and any express approval. Explain what the event offers without claiming that attendance satisfies an obligation automatically. Keep optional program learning separate from formal completion records.

items.title: The resource link is shared only inside a group
items.body: A group can introduce the resource, but the broader program should retain an appropriate open route. Staff should not need to join a presumed identity group to obtain useful learning. Preserve legitimate workspace permissions while removing an unnecessary learning-access barrier.

items.title: Members become the team’s permanent educators
items.body: A voluntary contribution should not turn into a standing duty to teach everyone about culture or equity. Use established courses, guidance and responsible expertise. Members can choose what to contribute within their roles, and staff throughout the team remain responsible for developing their own capability.

tabs.label: Learn
tabs.body: Learning identifies the idea and a relevant resource people can actually use. A discussion on the same topic as required training may be useful without satisfying its formal credit requirements. Describe its actual status and approval route accurately. Related One DSD resources remain available to staff; ERG membership does not create an invented learning gate.

tabs.label: Try
tabs.body: Trying an action connects the idea to work within the employee’s authority. A practice example can help practice identifying barriers without exposing restricted material. The employee should do the thinking and receive optional guidance where useful. Participation in a discussion alone does not demonstrate that the practice was applied or establish a person’s developmental orientation.

tabs.label: Reflect
tabs.body: Reflection asks what changed and what remains uncertain after the action. A revised instruction may look clearer yet still be difficult to use, so check an appropriate work result. Consultant guidance can help interpret evidence without taking over the employee’s responsibility. Keep a learning reflection distinct from a formal personnel judgment or a claim of required training completion.

check.question: A group hosts a discussion on a topic also found in required training. What should the leader say about credit?
check.correct: Explain the actual status and responsible approval route; do not assume the discussion automatically satisfies the required training.
wrong: Any event on the topic automatically counts as required training.
Only group members may access the related One DSD resources.
Attendance should determine the employee’s inferred developmental stage.
check.feedbackCorrect: This gives an accurate learning invitation while preserving formal training requirements and open access.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Topic overlap does not automatically confer required-training credit. Restricting related resources to members adds a learning gate the program does not require. Attendance cannot establish an assessed developmental stage. Explain the discussion’s actual status, preserve the responsible approval route for formal credit and keep staff learning openly available.

items.text: Use the discussion to practice writing a clearer project invitation.
Confirm whether responsible leadership expressly approved training credit.
Require group membership before someone may read the public learning resource.
Offer a related complete course and a work reflection.
Check the current formal requirement rather than infer credit from the topic.
Assign an individual IDI orientation from event attendance.

lessons.next: Next, review the contribution without overstating its effect.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: A group hosts a useful meeting on evidence-based decisions. Supervisor Andre announces that attendance satisfies every required equity training and that only members may use the related course. Neither statement has an actual authority basis.
options: Keep the promises to increase attendance.
Clarify the actual learning and credit status, provide the appropriate open resource route and offer a practical follow-through action.
Stop connecting group learning to work because credit is not automatic.
responses: Attendance incentives do not justify inaccurate claims or unnecessary access gates.
This preserves the useful connection while correcting credit and access assumptions.
Learning can be valuable without automatically replacing formal training.

lessons.transfer: Build a practice learning invitation with capability, complete resource, practice action, actual credit statement and open access route.

move.control: You can explain learning accurately and connect it to practical work without creating new participation gates.
move.failure: An optional event becomes an unsupported training claim or a condition of resource access.
move.next: Review the credit and access wording before the next learning invitation is shared.

lessons.title: Review contribution with honest evidence and follow-through
lessons.summary: Examine usefulness, access and decision response without turning membership into a personnel score.
lessons.objective: Choose evidence of a group’s contribution that fits a defined purpose.
objectives: Choose evidence of a group’s contribution that fits a defined purpose.
Identify an outcome claim that exceeds the available evidence.
Write an improvement with an owner, privacy limit and result check.
takeaways: A group does not guarantee every outcome.
lessons.statement: A credible review values the contribution while being honest about what remains unknown.

image.caption: Review usefulness and follow-through without profiling participants.

intro.heading: Examine what the contribution enabled
intro.body:
A leader may report success by counting events, attendees or messages. Those counts can describe activity, but they do not establish what people learned or what a decision changed. A useful review begins with the group’s purpose and asks what the contribution enabled. It should respect current reporting rules and avoid creating a personnel score from membership or attendance.

Choose a question that can be examined. Did participants understand a resource and find an appropriate next action? Did a process owner respond to a scoped suggestion? Could employees discover the participation route? These questions connect activity to usefulness without promising that a group alone will transform the entire workplace.

Use appropriate, minimal information. An unnamed quote may still identify a person when the event or role is distinctive. Small participation groups can be recognizable in a chart. Follow current responsible data and group reporting guidance rather than inventing a threshold, confidentiality promise or retention period. Use practice details for course practice and approved channels for real reporting.

Interpret outcomes cautiously. A change in workforce retention or engagement can have many influences. A resource group may contribute to the experience, but a simple timing comparison does not prove sole causation. Missing responses are not proof of no concern, and nonparticipation is not a measure of hostility or low commitment. Do not infer licensed IDI results from group activity.

Close the loop with a practical improvement. Explain what the evidence supports, which limit remains and who will take the next action. It might be a clearer invitation, an accessible material, a response from the process owner or a less burdensome support arrangement. The leader retains their responsibilities, the group retains its defined contribution, and staff build their own capability with guidance where helpful.

lessons.keyStatement: Report what the contribution enabled without turning attendance into a claim about people or a guarantee of outcomes.

items.title: Attendance increased
items.body: The count can describe participation when definitions and handling are appropriate. Ask what participants could use or do afterward. Do not inflate a larger event into proof that every workplace barrier disappeared. A useful review can preserve the count while adding a practical question about the purpose.

items.title: Retention improved during the same period
items.body: The timing may be relevant but does not establish that the group caused the result alone. Consider other workplace and external changes through responsible analysis. Describe the contribution with limits instead of promising the same outcome everywhere or making an unsupported causal claim.

items.title: Nonmembers receive a negative label
items.body: Membership and optional attendance do not establish commitment, culture or a developmental orientation. Employees may have different interests and constraints. Review the invitation and arrangement without turning participation into a hidden employment ranking or an access gate.

tabs.label: Purpose and finding
tabs.body: Purpose and finding connect the group’s contribution with relevant evidence. Events show activity; a documented design change can show consideration or influence; a workforce trend describes a different outcome. State each accurately. Lower departures after events may be encouraging, but do not alone establish that the group eliminated retention barriers.

tabs.label: Limit
tabs.body: A limit explains missing responses, privacy constraints and other influences on the result. Staffing, role mix and other workplace changes may occur alongside group activity. Silence cannot be filled with a no-concerns symbol, and nonattendance cannot establish low commitment. Honest limits protect the usefulness of the contribution rather than diminish it.

tabs.label: Next action
tabs.body: A next action identifies a manageable improvement and responsible owner. The leader might repair a response route or make an invitation clearer through applicable arrangements. Check whether the change became usable at the relevant point. Avoid a universal outcome promise or a personal participation ranking; the review should improve the relationship and work process.

check.question: A report says the group eliminated retention barriers because departures fell after several events. What is the responsible revision?
check.correct: Describe the observed activity and workforce change with definitions and limits, examine relevant process evidence and avoid claiming sole causation.
wrong: Make the claim stronger to demonstrate support.
Assign negative commitment scores to employees who did not attend.
Fill missing responses with a symbol meaning no concerns.
check.feedbackCorrect: This values the contribution while keeping the outcome claim within the evidence and preserving responsible handling.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A stronger success claim cannot repair missing causal evidence. Negative commitment scores invent meaning from optional nonattendance. A no-concerns symbol for missing responses creates false reassurance. Describe the actual contribution and observed change, explain limits and examine appropriate process evidence before deciding what to improve next.

items.text: The process owner adopted a clearer interest instruction after scoped input.
Attendance proves every member reached a particular IDI orientation.
Assign a responsible role to test the next invitation’s clarity.
The event introduced a resource; its later use has not yet been examined.
Nonmembers must be less committed to inclusion.
Explain which suggestion remains open and who will investigate it.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to support contribution, learning and credible response.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Director Amaya receives a group report showing several events and a suggestion that clarified a project invitation. Some survey responses are missing, and a small subgroup cannot be reported appropriately. Amaya wants to announce that every employee now feels included.
options: Report the activity and documented process change, state the limits and name the next usefulness check without a universal claim.
Treat missing responses as proof that no concerns remain.
Rank employees by whether they joined the group.
responses: This makes the real contribution visible while preserving accuracy, privacy and follow-through.
Missing information remains unknown and cannot support reassurance.
Membership is not a responsible basis for personal commitment or cultural labels.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice one-page group contribution review with purpose, activity, documented use, evidence limit, responsible owner and one improvement.

move.control: You can report contribution accurately and respond to process suggestions without profiling employees.
move.failure: A report celebrates counts and claims universal impact while uncertainty and follow-through disappear.
move.next: At the next appropriate review, connect one contribution to its result and identify one evidence-linked next action.

jobAid.subtitle: Support employee groups with clear purpose and credible response.
remember: Value contribution without claiming universal representation.
Use actual participation and formal-process requirements.
Report usefulness and limits without ranking employees.

sections.heading: Understand and arrange
items: Read the current group purpose, rules and responsible contact route.
Explain contribution without compulsory cultural education.
Check current participation, leadership and time requirements through appropriate guidance.
Discuss practical work arrangements without identity assumptions or unsupported promises.

sections.heading: Support and invite
items: Ask what leader support would be useful.
Name the action, authority limit and follow-through owner.
Offer input while the choice can still change and state constraints honestly.
Respond to suggestions, disagreement and unresolved questions in plain language.

sections.heading: Learn and review
items: Connect learning to a practical capability and an appropriate open resource route.
Keep required training credit distinct from optional activity unless expressly approved.
Use approved information and current privacy guidance.
Separate activity, usefulness and causal claims.
Never infer individual IDI orientations or hidden commitment scores from membership or attendance.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Minnesota employee resource groups
sources.note: Current public enterprise program entry point; use its actual group information rather than an invented local membership or schedule.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Enterprise ERG Guidelines
sources.note: Explains public purpose and governance, including distinctions from bargaining and grievance functions. The support plans in the course are learning choices.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Enterprise ERG FAQs
sources.note: Actual participation, leadership, time and approval questions require current guidance and responsible agency advice; no blanket rule is created here.

sources.title: Minnesota DHS — Equity Policy
sources.note: Agency equity responsibilities remain with their responsible roles and required processes. Group input does not replace required analysis or formal review.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited Policy 1436
sources.note: Protected-class harassment and discrimination concerns use formal procedures. Managers and supervisors must immediately report allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer; optional support does not replace that duty.
